opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think about this question almost every day. When I look at where Meshy is today, I see us at the very beginning of a much longer curve.

The first thing is the market itself. Right now, 3D content creation is still a skill held by a relatively small number of professionals: game artists, VFX people, industrial designers. It takes years to learn Blender or Maya, and making a single high-quality asset can take days. So the 3D market today is actually constrained by the supply of people who can make 3D. If we bring the cost of creating a 3D asset down by 10x, 100x, then the market isn't just the existing 3D artists anymore. It's everyone who has an idea. Look at what happened with photography when smartphones came out, or with video when TikTok made editing trivial. The number of creators exploded by orders of magnitude. I believe 3D can go through the same transition, and that's where the 100x comes from.

The second thing is technology. The models are improving incredibly fast. When we started, generated meshes were pretty rough. You could use them as a starting point, but you'd still spend a lot of time cleaning them up. Now the geometry, the textures, the topology are getting much closer to production-ready. And I think within a few years, the gap between AI-generated and hand-made assets will be very small for a lot of use cases. Once quality crosses that threshold, adoption doesn't grow linearly. It jumps.

Third is new use cases that don't really exist yet. 3D printing is one I'm very excited about. A lot of people want to print something personalized: a figurine of their pet, a custom toy for their kid. Before, the bottleneck was always "where do I get the model?" Now you can just describe it or upload a photo. Then there's AR/VR, embodied AI and robotics simulation, which need enormous amounts of 3D data, and eventually maybe fully AI-generated games and virtual worlds. Each of these could be bigger than the traditional game-asset market.

And finally, it comes down to execution and team. My background is in computer graphics; I built Taichi during my PhD at MIT. One lesson I took from that is that the tools that win are the ones people actually love to use. So we stay very close to our users, ship fast, and try to make the product genuinely useful rather than just a demo. If we keep doing that while the technology and the market both expand, I think 100x is quite realistic, and 1,000x is about whether we can help 3D become a medium that everyone uses, the way images and video are today.

That's really the mission: let anyone bring their imagination into 3D.

r001.rationale: The response forecasts 100x–1,000x growth and explains drivers for it; it does not say growth can emerge incrementally without the founder anticipating its scale.

r002.rationale: The response discusses improving technology and staying close to users, but does not describe revising or overturning the founder’s own understanding.

r003.rationale: It names potential new 3D use cases, but does not explain that providing programmable computing capacity lets users discover applications the creator did not anticipate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that Meshy gets 100 or 1,000 times bigger only if 3D stops being a niche skill and becomes something everyone does, the way photos and video already are.

Right now, 3D is gated by tooling. If you want a character or an environment, you need someone who knows Blender or Maya, and that person spends days on a single asset. That means almost all 3D content in the world is made by a few million professionals, mostly in games and film. Meshy today mostly serves those people and the indie developers next to them. That's a real business, but it's a ceiling.

The way through that ceiling is to collapse the cost of making a 3D asset to roughly the cost of describing it. When you can type a sentence or upload a sketch and get a usable, rigged, textured model in a minute, the user base changes. It's not just studios anymore. It's a kid making a Roblox map, a furniture store generating product views, an architect blocking out a scene, a teacher building a lesson. Each of those is a market larger than professional 3D on its own.

The second piece is where those assets go. Games are the obvious destination, but I think the bigger long-term pull is from things that don't exist at scale yet: AR glasses, robotics simulation, world models that need huge amounts of 3D training data. All of them are hungry for geometry, and nobody has a cheap supply of it today. If Meshy becomes the default place that supply comes from, growth stops being about marketing and starts being about demand we don't have to create.

On the execution side, the thing I care most about is quality compounding. Every generation that a user keeps or fixes teaches the model something. We have millions of users doing that now, and that flywheel is the moat. Compute gets cheaper, models get better, and the gap between "looks fine in a demo" and "I'd ship this" keeps shrinking. Once it closes for most use cases, pricing and distribution take over, and that's when the step function happens.

So, 100x is making 3D creation accessible to everyone who wants it. 1,000x is becoming the infrastructure layer that every spatial product, from games to robots, pulls from. We're early on both, but the direction is clear.

r001.rationale: The candidate lays out an intentional path to 100x and 1,000x growth; it does not describe growth emerging incrementally without the founder anticipating the scale.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not describe revising or overturning its understanding as part of building the business.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses 3D asset generation and possible markets, but not providing programmable computing capacity that lets users discover unforeseen applications.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make 3D creation useful to many more people. If we only help existing 3D artists work faster, that’s valuable, but to grow 100 or 1,000 times, we need to reach people who have ideas but don’t have the skills or time to learn traditional 3D tools.

That means making the whole process easier. You should be able to describe what you want, iterate on it, and get something you can actually use in a game, a video, or a physical product. Generating a model is one step; getting it into your project is what makes it valuable.

So I’d focus on two things: improving the quality and controllability of the technology, and understanding where people get stuck in real workflows. If we can close that gap, we can expand both who creates 3D content and how much they create. That’s where I see the potential for that kind of growth.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reaching much larger scale through broader access and better workflows, but does not say growth can emerge incrementally without the founder anticipating its eventual scale.

r002.rationale: It recommends improving technology and understanding user workflows, but does not identify revising or overturning one’s own understanding as part of building a business.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss providing programmable computing capacity or users discovering unanticipated applications.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make 3D creation useful to many more people. If we only make the existing workflow faster for professional artists, that’s valuable, but it probably isn’t enough to grow 100 or 1,000 times. We need to help people who have an idea but don’t have the skills or time to build it in 3D.

That means improving both the quality of the models and how easily people can use them. Generating something that looks good is one step. Getting it into a game, an animation, or another project is where the value becomes real.

So I would focus on two things: making the technology better and understanding where users get stuck. If we can take someone from “I have an idea” to “I made something I can actually use,” we can expand the number of people who create in 3D. That’s where I see the potential for that kind of growth.
